title: Kayla Hamilton Act
official_title: To amend the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 to enhance efforts to combat the trafficking of children.
summary: The Kayla Hamilton Act tightens the placement process for unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody. It requires the Department of Health and Human Services to place children 13 and older in a secure facility if they have gang-related tattoos, markings, or an arrest record linked to gang activity in their home country. It also prohibits placing any child with a sponsor who is unlawfully present in the U.S., and requires DHS to receive detailed background information on all adult household members at any placement home.
brief: Requires secure facility placement for unaccompanied migrant children 13 and older with gang-related indicators, bans placement with sponsors who are unlawfully present, and mandates sharing of household adult background information with DHS.

top_lines.headline: Secure Facility for Gang-Affiliated Minors
subs: Before placing an unaccompanied child 13 or older, HHS must contact the child's home country consulate or embassy to request the child's criminal record
HHS must also examine the child for gang-related tattoos and markings
If the child has a gang-related tattoo, marking, or a gang-related arrest record or criminal conviction from their home country, HHS must place them in a secure facility

top_lines.headline: Sponsor Vetting Requirements
subs: No child may be placed with a sponsor who is unlawfully present in the United States

Before placement, HHS must share with DHS: names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, immigration status, contact information, and background check results for all adult residents of the placement household
Required background checks include a sex offender registry check, a public records check, and an FBI fingerprint-based criminal history check for every adult in the household

likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and was received in the Senate in December 2025, but has only 2 cosponsors and no Senate companion bill visible. Democrats have broadly opposed bills that restrict HHS placement flexibility for unaccompanied migrant children, and the 60-vote threshold for Senate floor consideration makes bipartisan support essential. No Senate committee action has been reported.

items.main: Names the Act the “Kayla Hamilton Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Additional Safeguards for Placement of Unaccompanied Children

items.main: For unaccompanied migrant children aged 13 and older, requires HHS to request a criminal record from the child's home country consulate or embassy and conduct a gang marking examination before making any placement.
items.detail: If the child has a gang-related tattoo, any other gang-related marking, or a home-country arrest record, pending charge, or conviction related to gang affiliation, HHS must place the child in a secure facility. The bill exempts children aged 12 or younger from the gang-screening requirement. The Secretary is not required to review placement in a secure facility under this provision.

items.main: Prohibits placement of any unaccompanied child with a sponsor who is unlawfully present in the United States, and requires HHS to transmit detailed household information to DHS before completing any placement.
items.detail: Required information includes names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, immigration status, contact information, and background check results for all adult residents of the proposed placement household. Background checks must include a Department of Justice National Sex Offender public website check, a public records background check, and an FBI National Criminal History fingerprint-based check. The amendment also changes 'may consider' to 'shall consider' in making placement determinations, converting a discretionary consideration into a mandatory one.

underreported.section: Section 2 — Change from 'May Consider' to 'Shall Consider'
underreported.summary: Changes the HHS placement standard from permitting consideration of placement-determination factors to requiring that consideration, by striking 'may consider' and inserting 'shall consider'. This makes the assessment a mandatory step in placement determinations, rather than a discretionary one.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose focuses on gang screening and sponsor vetting. This separate textual change — from 'may' to 'shall' — alters the baseline placement standard for all unaccompanied children regardless of gang affiliation, broadening the scope of the bill beyond its headline provisions.

gaps: The bill requires HHS to contact a child's home country consulate for a criminal record before placement, but does not establish a timeline for how long HHS may hold a child while awaiting a response, or what happens if the consulate does not respond.

The bill prohibits placement with sponsors who are unlawfully present but does not address what happens to a child if no lawful placement is available, potentially requiring indefinite secure facility detention.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Jayapal
featured_quotes.text: let me just remind the majority that the Office of Refugee Resettlement subjects all potential sponsors of unaccompanied kids to an assessment. That assessment includes numerous factors, including the sponsor's relationship to the child, the sponsor's motivation for seeking to care for the child, and any special vulnerabilities that the child has.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Rivas
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, the bill we are debating today is a bad bill. It is a bad bill that will harm vulnerable children, do nothing to fix our immigration system, and embolden Trump to continue wreaking havoc in our communities. Republicans are exploiting a tragedy to push forth a bill that undermines and strips away critical rights and protections for vulnerable children. H.R. 4371 treats immigrant children like criminals and prevents unaccompanied minors from being reunited with their families.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Ramirez
featured_quotes.text: we are less than 10 days away from Christmas, a day in which many celebrate the birth of Jesus, a refugee. In regard to the hypocrisy of those who would quote Scripture asserting the preciousness of children while they pursue new, cruel punishments for child refugees, I find that not just hypocritical but despicable. This administration and the Republicans have used their power not to protect children but, instead, to strip unaccompanied children who come to this country fleeing danger, looking for safety or protection.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Stansbury
featured_quotes.text: Let me begin by saying what should be clear to every Member of this body: The murder of Kayla Hamilton is a horrific and truly heartbreaking tragedy, and no family should ever have to endure such a loss. Nothing that we can do or say here will diminish the pain of those who loved her.

added: Mandatory consulate/embassy criminal record request for unaccompanied children aged 13 and older before placement
Mandatory gang tattoo and marking examination before placement for children aged 13 and older
Mandatory secure facility placement for children aged 13 and older with gang-related indicators
Prohibition on placement with sponsors who are unlawfully present in the United States
Requirement to transmit household adult background check results to DHS before each placement
modified: 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(2): 'may consider' changed to 'shall consider' in making placement determinations

added: New Sec. 2 amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 279(b)(2)) so ORR placement determinations must follow 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(2)
New mandatory consultation step with DHS and the Attorney General before any placement, to assess flight risk, danger, and criminal history
Express prohibition on releasing an unaccompanied alien child on his or her own recognizance
Detailed secure-facility placement rules for children 12 or older who are a flight risk or danger, including serious-offense, aggravated-felony, and gang-activity triggers (with INA cross-references)

New subparagraph (D) listing 11 categories of individuals a child may not be placed with, including non-citizens/non-LPRs and those (or household members) convicted of sex, trafficking, domestic violence, child abuse, murder, or felony offenses
New Sec. 5 exempting agencies from the Paperwork Reduction Act and Administrative Procedure Act where compliance would impede immediate implementation
New Sec. 6 effective-date/applicability provision covering pending and post-enactment custody determinations and all release redeterminations
modified: Background-check requirement (paragraph (3)(D)(vii)) renamed the registry to the "Dru Sjodin National Sex Offender Public Website" and now also accepts an individual taxpayer identification number; the introduced version cited the DOJ National Sex Offender public website and required a social security number
Gang/criminal-record screening restructured: child-12-or-younger carve-out replaced with rules applying to children "12 years of age or older"
Bill purpose expanded to also amend the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (introduced amended only the Wilberforce Act)
removed: Introduced text's standalone "a child shall not be placed with an individual who is unlawfully present in the United States" sentence in paragraph (3)(A) is replaced by the broader citizen/LPR requirement in the new (D)
